about: Roles shown on the GEO board, by NORAD catalogue number. An object is listed only where published reporting supports the role; each entry cites it. Unlisted objects have no listed role, which says nothing about what they are. Each entry says whether its role is declared (by the operator or the state) or attributed (by analysts, tracking firms or another government, named in the basis), and gives a status with the date of the newest source behind it. Curated by hand; checked 26 Oct 2026, widened from Secure World Foundation's RPO sheet and every source re-read 27 Nov 2026 (docs/validation/geo-board.md).

roles.inspection: Inspection-capable: publicly reported rendezvous, proximity operations or inspection of other satellites
roles.servicing: Servicing: docks with client satellites (life extension or refuelling)

claims.declared: The role is the operator's or the state's own description of the satellite
claims.attributed: The role is an assessment by analysts, tracking firms or another government, named in the basis

statuses.active: Reported operating or manoeuvring as of the status date
statuses.retired: Reported decommissioned, passivated or broken up as of the status date
statuses.uncertain: No recent report: the status date is that of the newest source found

objects.name: LUCH-5X (OLYMP-K 2)
objects.basis: Moved along the belt after its March 2023 launch, stopping near commercial satellites; closest measured about 16 km (Slingshot Aerospace)
objects.status_note: Left 62° E between 15 Oct and 22 Nov 2026 in Space-Track's element sets, as Orbit measured them (docs/validation/luch2-relocations.md)

objects.name: USA 270 (GSSAP 3)
objects.basis: US Space Force GSSAP satellite (launched Aug 2016). The programme tracks and characterises objects in geosynchronous orbit, and its satellites can manoeuvre to observe objects at close range or conduct rendezvous (Air & Space Forces Magazine's programme page)
objects.status_note: Listed 'on orbit, active' by Air & Space Forces Magazine (undated page, read 27 Nov 2026); Designation-Systems.net (updated 15 Feb 2026) counts seven of eight GSSAP satellites active, USA 254 being the one retired

objects.name: SHIJIAN-17 (SJ-17)
objects.basis: Chinese satellite (launched 3 Nov 2016) that China declared a test of advanced technologies. Secure World Foundation's fact sheet reports that it circumnavigated ChinaSat-5A at 50 to 100 km in Nov 2016, closing to within a few km on 30 Nov; came within 1.5 km of ChinaSat-1C on 29 Jul 2018, which it says strongly suggests an inspection; made RPO with ChinaSat-6B and Shijian-20 in Jan and Oct 2020; and spent a brief period next to VENESAT-1 in Nov 2023. The Space Review (Mowthorpe and Trichas, Aug 2022) reports the approaches to 2020; Defense One (May 2024) says it began approaching satellites, French, Russian and Indonesian among them, shortly after its checkout in 2016
objects.status_note: Moving from Feb 2023; dropped below the belt on 1 Nov 2024, rejoined it on 14 Nov and entered the Western hemisphere on 20 Nov 2024, and appears stable at 178° W (Secure World Foundation fact sheet, Jun 2026)
sources: Secure World Foundation fact sheet: Chinese military and intelligence RPO, Jun 2026

objects.name: SHIJIAN-21 (SJ-21)
objects.basis: Docked with the defunct BeiDou-2 G2 and towed it about 3,000 km above GEO in January 2022; reported docked with Shijian-25 in 2025 by tracking firms, and separated from it in mid-January 2026 (an ISR University newsletter, quoted by China in Space); China has not confirmed the 2025 docking
objects.status_note: Manoeuvring after the separation from Shijian-25 in January 2026 (China in Space, 26 Jan 2026)

objects.name: SHIJIAN-25 (SJ-25)
objects.basis: Built to test refuelling and life extension; tracking firms reported it docked with Shijian-21 in mid-2025 (not confirmed by China); the pair separated in mid-January 2026 (an ISR University newsletter, quoted by China in Space)
objects.status_note: In geostationary orbit after the separation from Shijian-21 (China in Space, 26 Jan 2026)

objects.name: MEV-1
objects.basis: Northrop Grumman Mission Extension Vehicle: docks with client satellites to extend their life; served Intelsat 901 from Feb 2020 and undocked on 9 Apr 2025
objects.status_note: Undocked from Intelsat 901 on 9 Apr 2025 (Northrop Grumman and Intelsat, as Wikipedia gives them); Wikipedia says it then went to serve Optus D3, and SatNews reported a Mission Extension Vehicle undocking from Optus D3 on 12 Aug 2026 without naming which

objects.name: MEV-2
objects.basis: Northrop Grumman Mission Extension Vehicle; docked to Intelsat 10-02 on 12 Apr 2021; on 23 May 2024 Northrop Grumman said it would stay docked for four more years
objects.status_note: Docked to Intelsat 10-02, with service extended by four years (Northrop Grumman, 23 May 2024)

objects.name: USA 253 (GSSAP 1)
objects.basis: US Space Force GSSAP satellite (launched 28 Jul 2014). The programme tracks and characterises objects in geosynchronous orbit, and its satellites can manoeuvre to observe objects at close range or conduct rendezvous (Air & Space Forces Magazine's programme page)
objects.status_note: Listed 'on orbit, active' by Air & Space Forces Magazine (undated page, read 27 Nov 2026); Designation-Systems.net (updated 15 Feb 2026) counts seven of eight GSSAP satellites active, USA 254 being the one retired
sources: Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)

objects.name: USA 254 (GSSAP 2)
objects.basis: US Space Force GSSAP satellite (launched 28 Jul 2014), in the programme that tracks and characterises objects in geosynchronous orbit and can manoeuvre to observe them at close range (Air & Space Forces Magazine's programme page). Decommissioned in 2023: Space Operations Command announced it out of service on 2 Aug 2023, and Space Systems Command said on 14 Aug 2023 it was passivated and in a graveyard orbit
objects.status_note: Passivated and in a graveyard orbit (Space Systems Command, 14 Aug 2023, reported by SpaceNews); Air & Space Forces Magazine lists it 'nonoperational orbit, decommissioned in 2023'
sources: Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)

objects.name: USA 255 (ANGELS)
objects.basis: AFRL experiment launched with GSSAP 1 and 2 on 28 Jul 2014: manoeuvred around its own Delta IV upper stage, several hundred km above GEO, from about 50 km to within several km (AFRL fact sheet, as Wikipedia gives it); from Jul 2016 the 3rd Space Experimentation Squadron flew it for threat replication trajectories (Gunter's Space Page)
objects.status_note: Decommissioned in Nov 2017 (Gunter's Space Page, cited by Wikipedia)
sources: Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)

objects.name: LUCH (OLYMP-K 1)
objects.basis: Russian satellite (launched 28 Sep 2014); Russia has made no official claim about its mission. SpaceNews reported it parked between Intelsat 901 and Intelsat 7 from Apr 2015 and beside Intelsat 905 from Sep 2015; on 7 Sep 2018 France's armed forces minister said it had approached Athena-Fidus in 2017 and called that espionage. Secure World Foundation lists it parked near Express, Intelsat and Athena-Fidus satellites from Oct 2014
objects.status_note: Decommissioned and moved to a graveyard orbit above GEO in Oct 2025; appeared to break apart on 30 Jan 2026 in s2a systems' optical imagery (Space.com, 30 Jan 2026)
sources: Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)

objects.name: TJS-3
objects.basis: Chinese satellite (launched Dec 2018) whose programme name means communication technology test; what the US suspects is a counterspace satellite (Breaking Defense, Oct 2021). Orbital Focus and Satellite Dashboard data show it drifting from Jul 2022 and stopping near USA 233 (13 Sep 2022; as close as 6.2 km on 31 Oct 2022) and USA 298 (8 Feb 2023) (Space.com, Mar 2023). Secure World Foundation lists approaches to Russian and US satellites from May 2019 and RPO with TJS-10 from Nov 2023 to Nov 2024
objects.status_note: Secure World Foundation's sheet (updated 17 Feb 2026) says it started moving again after Nov 2024; no later report found
sources: Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)

objects.name: TJS-3 AKM (TJS-3's companion)
objects.basis: Catalogued as TJS-3's apogee kick motor, but kept station in step with TJS-3 on 4 and 11 Jan 2019 and matched its manoeuvres (Bob Hall's Spacecast, Jul 2019, as Wikipedia gives it); in May 2019 TJS-3 left and this object took its place, which COMSPOC's Jim Cooper read as practice at spoofing other nations' space surveillance (Breaking Defense, Oct 2021). Defense One (May 2024) says the two conducted RPO during a checkout phase. China has not acknowledged a second object; Gunter's Space Page calls it a subsatellite
objects.status_note: No activity after May 2019 reported in the sources found; the newest is Defense One, 20 May 2024
sources: Gunter's Space Page: TJS 3 / TJS 3 Subsatellite
Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)

objects.name: SHIYAN 12 01 (SY-12 01)
objects.basis: Chinese test satellite launched with SY-12 02 on 23 Dec 2021. SpaceNews (Jun 2022) calls the pair 'Chinese inspection satellites'; Defense One (May 2024), citing Satellite Dashboard, says both approached several foreign communications satellites shortly after reaching GEO. When USA 270 (GSSAP 3) approached in early 2022 the pair left in opposite directions (COMSPOC, reported by SpaceNews); Defense One lists this one as having moved to avoid observation
objects.status_note: No activity after early 2022 reported in the sources found; the newest is Defense One, 20 May 2024
sources: SpaceNews: An in-orbit game of cat and mouse
Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)

objects.name: SHIYAN 12 02 (SY-12 02)
objects.basis: Chinese test satellite launched with SY-12 01 on 23 Dec 2021. SpaceNews (Jun 2022) calls the pair 'Chinese inspection satellites'; Defense One (May 2024), citing Satellite Dashboard, says both approached several foreign communications satellites shortly after reaching GEO. When USA 270 (GSSAP 3) approached in early 2022 the pair left in opposite directions, and on 14 Feb 2022 this one put itself between the Sun and USA 270, which COMSPOC's caption calls an imaging opportunity (SpaceNews); Secure World Foundation says it 'apparently' got one
objects.status_note: No activity after early 2022 reported in the sources found; the newest is Defense One, 20 May 2024
sources: SpaceNews: An in-orbit game of cat and mouse
Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)

objects.name: LINUSS2
objects.basis: One of Lockheed Martin's two LINUSS 12U CubeSats, taken to GEO on USSF-44 in Nov 2022. Lockheed Martin said on 18 Apr 2023 that one CubeSat acted as the servicing vehicle and navigated toward the other; Breaking Defense reports imagery at 400 m on 28 Feb 2023. Neither says which CubeSat was the servicer: Secure World Foundation's sheet names LINUSS2 as servicer and LINUSS1 as client. No docking was reported, so the role is inspection, not servicing
objects.status_note: Breaking Defense (17 Apr 2023) said tests would run for the satellites' lifetime, first projected at about a year; no later report found
sources: Aviation Week: LINUSS rendezvous within 400 m
Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)

objects.name: LDPE-3A
objects.basis: US military Long Duration Propulsive ESPA vehicle (launched 15 Jan 2023 on USSF-67) hosting space situational awareness payloads, among them WASSAT, a wide-area camera for tracking objects in GEO (Gunter's Space Page). Gunter's Space Page says it began shadowing China's Shijian-23 in Oct 2024, that a close approach at about 30 km 'may have happened' on 4 and 5 Nov 2024, and that it then synchronised its drift with Shijian-23. Secure World Foundation's row cites that page; no other report was found
objects.status_note: No activity after Nov 2024 reported; Gunter's Space Page (updated 27 Aug 2026) gives no later status
sources: Secure World Foundation, RPO data of the Global Counterspace Capabilities report (sheet updated 17 Feb 2026)
